name: Soul-Jazz Roots
description: Soul jazz blended hard bop with blues, gospel and rhythm and blues, most often in small combos and organ trios built around the Hammond organ. Jimmy Smith did more than anyone to establish the Hammond B-3 as a jazz and soul instrument, and Blue Note was the style's central label. In Memphis over the same years, the Stax house band was cutting all-instrumental soul singles that worked the same earthy, blues-based feel.
characteristics: Tenor sax and guitar front lines

name: Classic Funk
description: James Brown's run of records from "Papa's Got a Brand New Bag" (1965) through "Cold Sweat" (1967) and "Sex Machine" (1970) is what pulled funk out of soul and made it its own form: a static one- or two-chord vamp, heavy emphasis on the first beat, syncopated basslines and guitar riffs, melody pushed to the back. New Orleans arrived at its own version through the Meters. The 1970s were the decade of funk's highest mainstream visibility.
characteristics: Drums and bass locked as one part

name: Jazz-Funk
description: Jazz musicians took up the funk backbeat along with electric keyboards, bass guitar and analog synthesizers, keeping improvisation in the arrangement. Miles Davis's On the Corner and Jimmy Smith's Root Down, both 1972, are cited as early landmarks; Herbie Hancock played ARP Odyssey and clavinet on Head Hunters in 1973. The range ran from open jazz improvisation to soul, funk and disco played with jazz arrangements.
characteristics: Electric bass in the lead role

name: P-Funk & Boogie
description: George Clinton's Parliament produced a funk heavily coloured by jazz and psychedelic rock, and Mothership Connection (1975) became the band's first gold and later platinum record. Bernie Worrell's keyboards and Bootsy Collins's bass defined the sound, with Maceo Parker and Fred Wesley bringing the James Brown horn language across. From the late 1970s into the mid 1980s, boogie carried the same lineage into electronic dance music, built on mid-tempo grooves, slap bass, synthesizers and an accent on the second and fourth beats.

name: Rare Groove Revival
description: "Rare groove" was coined by the British DJ Norman Jay, whose Original Rare Groove Show on pirate station Kiss FM in the 1980s traded in obscure American funk, R&B and jazz-funk records. The same records fed hip-hop production through sampling. In Brooklyn the revival turned into new recordings: Daptone Records, founded in 2001 by Gabriel Roth and Neal Sugarman, kept computers out of the studio in favour of analog tape, and Truth & Soul followed in 2004.
characteristics: 45 rpm singles as the primary format

name: The New Pocket
description: Funk-soul bands formed in the 2010s built their audiences online and released through their own labels rather than through the industry. Vulfpeck, formed in Ann Arbor in 2011, put out four EPs before its debut album and has issued everything on its own Vulf Records. The playing is deliberately spare, with the rhythm section treated as the whole point of the record.
characteristics: Bass and drums as the lead voice
